title: Ontological Instability and the Internal Author in the Fiction of Philip K. Dick
author: Ciarán Kavanagh
card_summary: A Master of Arts thesis from the National University of Ireland, Cork, examining ontological instability and the concept of the internal author in Philip K. Dick's fiction. Explores how Dick's narratives destabilize the reader's sense of reality and embed authorial self-reflection within the fictional world.
works_discussed: The Man in the High Castle

## **Introduction** 

- _“. . . you were supposed to draw him into our world, the shared reality of our society . . . instead,_ 

_hasn't he drawn you into his own?”_ 

( _Martian Time-slip_ 139) 

The world of Philip K. Dick is situated, quite hazardously, on a boundary. This boundary is not clear-cut; at its most visible it is blurred, at its least it is barely extant. It is the boundary between two worlds, the world of fiction and the world of reality. While none of us can claim to live free of fiction, completely grounded in objective reality, Philip K. Dick is an exemplar, perhaps _the_ exemplar, of the protean ‘between’ space.
